title: Speakers of Sport v. ProServ
summary: A rival sports agent’s optimistic prediction about endorsements did not establish the fraudulent promise needed for the former agent’s interference claim.

sections.Parties: Speakers of Sport, Ivan Rodriguez’s former agent, sued competing agency ProServ. Rodriguez was the client whose move supplied the alleged interference.
sections.Material Facts:
Rodriguez had one-year agreements with Speakers that were terminable at will. ProServ recruited him in 1995 and said it could obtain between $2 million and $4 million in endorsements. He changed agencies. ProServ obtained no significant endorsements, and a year later Rodriguez changed agents again. Speakers alleged that the endorsement promise was fraudulent and induced the termination of its relationship.

The promised endorsement income would have come from third-party businesses. There was no contention that Rodriguez understood ProServ to guarantee a minimum payment from its own funds if endorsements failed to materialize.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered summary judgment for ProServ. The Seventh Circuit affirmed. The excerpt addresses the characterization of the representation within the former agent’s claim, rather than a damages action by Rodriguez on an express minimum-payment guarantee.
sections.Issue: Did ProServ’s recruitment statement constitute an actionable fraudulent commitment rather than an aspirational sales representation?
sections.Holding: On this record, no. The court treated it as an optimistic statement that ProServ would try to obtain endorsements; it also found the alleged promise alone insufficient to establish the required fraudulent scheme.
sections.Reasoning:
An at-will client can move between competing agents without breaching an obligation to remain. Competition may justify conduct that would otherwise be alleged as interference, although the privilege does not authorize fraud. The court was concerned that treating every unrealized prediction of better results as evidence of fraud would subject ordinary competitive recruitment to substantial litigation risk.

The meaning of the representation depended on context. ProServ could seek endorsements but could not compel advertisers to pay. A party can assume responsibility for events outside its control through a warranty; the court expressly recognized that possibility. Here, however, there was no plausible showing that ProServ promised to make up a shortfall itself. The figures expressed an aspiration for third-party business rather than a guaranteed return.

The court gave an alternative reason: even assuming a promise or warranty, the asserted fraud was not supported by evidence of a broader fraudulent scheme beyond that promise. The result should not be generalized into a rule that promises about outside events can never bind.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It helps distinguish a legally assumed risk, an optimistic prediction, and a promise made with fraudulent intent.

topics.promise: The court interpreted the endorsement figures as aspiration rather than a payment guarantee.
topics.misrepresentation: Failure to achieve predicted results did not itself establish actionable fraud.
topics.assent: Objective context determined the nature of the apparent commitment.
topics.discretion: An undertaking to try to obtain business differs from guaranteeing a fixed financial result.

mnemonic.rationale: A sports agent and a rival’s promise
